explanations.explanation: Hezekiah, Judah's king, says, “I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand from me.” That's a blank check, friend. It's like telling a stranger "name your number" and then holding your breath. Sennacherib, Assyria's king, names it in the very next line.

explanations.answer: To hand over his own throne
explanations.explanation: No throne in this offer, friend. Hezekiah, Judah's king, says, “…I will pay whatever you demand from me.” Nothing he says mentions giving up his seat. What he puts on the table is payment, and he asks Assyria to withdraw.

explanations.answer: To send troops for his wars
explanations.explanation: Troops never come up in his message. Hezekiah, Judah's king, asks the king of Assyria to withdraw and says, “…I will pay whatever you demand from me.” His offer is money, plain and simple. Nobody is signing up for anybody's army here.

explanations.answer: The LORD's house and the palace treasuries
explanations.explanation: Hezekiah hands over all the silver that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace. That's two buildings emptied out. It's like turning over every coat pocket and couch cushion you own, then the neighbor's too. Hezekiah, Judah's king, is trying to pay the whole bill.

explanations.answer: The cities of the Philistines he defeated
explanations.explanation: The text sends us somewhere closer to home. The silver comes from the house of the LORD and the treasuries of the royal palace. No Philistine cities are mentioned in this payment. Hezekiah, Judah's king, is digging through his own buildings.

explanations.answer: The ships that came in from Tarshish
explanations.explanation: No ships pull into this story, friend. The silver is what was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace. Hezekiah, Judah's king, scrapes together everything those two places have. If a cargo ship had shown up, it would have been a much easier day.

Gold it is. Hezekiah stripped the gold he had plated on the doors and doorposts of the temple of the LORD. Think about that. It's like peeling the shine right off your own front door to cover a bill. Hezekiah, Judah's king, is giving up what he had put there himself.

Close in the metal family, but the text says gold. Hezekiah stripped the gold with which he had plated the doors and doorposts of the temple of the LORD. Then he gave it to the king of Assyria. Hezekiah, Judah's king, is the one who had put that gold on there in the first place.

Cedar is a fine wood, but the verse names something shinier. Hezekiah stripped the gold with which he had plated the doors and doorposts of the temple of the LORD. The doors stay, and the gold goes to the king of Assyria. It's the plating that comes off.

I wish that were how it went, friend. The text says, “Nevertheless, the king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh, along with a great army…” Those are three of his officials, and they head for Jerusalem. Hezekiah paid, and Assyria still sends an army his way.

Right, and that's the sting of it. The text says, “Nevertheless, the king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh, along with a great army…” Hezekiah, Judah's king, had already paid. Think of a bill you paid in full that still shows up in the mailbox.

Not this time, friend. The text says, “Then they called for the king.” But it's three of his men who went out to them: Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebnah the scribe and Joah the recorder. Hezekiah, Judah's king, sends his men and stays put.

Yes, he doesn't go out. The Assyrians called for the king, and Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebnah the scribe and Joah the recorder went out to them. So the army asks for the king and gets his staff. That's like asking to see the manager and getting three people from the front desk.

He asks, “What is the basis of this confidence of yours?” Basis means what it's standing on. Hezekiah's confidence is under the microscope, and the Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, wants to see the foundation. He opens with a question, and a pointed one.

He never asks about how long. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, asks, “What is the basis of this confidence of yours?” He wants to know what Hezekiah's confidence stands on. It's a question about the foundation, not the timer.

explanations.answer: Who it is meant to impress
explanations.explanation: Nobody's being impressed in his question. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, asks, “What is the basis of this confidence of yours?” He's asking what Hezekiah's confidence is based on. It's less about the audience and all about the foundation.

Egypt is the one he names. He says, “Look now, you are trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it.” He also names Pharaoh king of Egypt. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, has his guess ready, and it comes with a picture.
Babylon doesn't come up here, friend. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “Look now, you are trusting in Egypt…” He goes on to mention Pharaoh king of Egypt. Egypt is the name in his mouth.
Moab isn't in this speech. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “Look now, you are trusting in Egypt…” He even adds Pharaoh king of Egypt to the picture. It's Egypt he points at.

He does say it. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, asks, “…is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem: ‘You must worship before this altar in Jerusalem’?” That's his answer ready for anyone who says they trust the LORD. He's bringing up what Hezekiah did and quoting him back.

It's right there in the verse. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, asks, “…is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed…” He goes on to quote Hezekiah telling Judah and Jerusalem to worship before the altar in Jerusalem. So the Rabshakeh does bring it up, and he brings it up on purpose.

explanations.answer: Judah has to find riders for them
explanations.explanation: Here's the catch: “…if you can put riders on them!” Two thousand horses sounds generous until you see the fine print. It's like being given a free car when you don't have a driver. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, is poking at Judah with this one.

explanations.answer: Judah has to pay for every horse
explanations.explanation: No price per horse gets named. The catch is in the last part of his offer: “…if you can put riders on them!” The horses are the easy part. Finding two thousand riders is the hard part, and the Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, knows it.

explanations.answer: Judah has to return them by spring
explanations.explanation: No return date in this deal, friend. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “…if you can put riders on them!” That's the whole catch. Judah would need two thousand riders to go with two thousand horses.

The LORD is the name he uses. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’” That's what he claims. Notice he's trying to take the very thing Hezekiah is leaning on and use it against him.

Baal isn't the name in his mouth. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’” He uses the LORD's name, which is why this line stands out. It's the boldest thing he's said so far.

Dagon doesn't make an appearance here, friend. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’” He names the LORD, and that's the bold part. It's the claim to watch.

They ask, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it. Do not speak with us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall.” Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebnah the scribe and Joah the recorder are the three speaking. I think they wanted this talk kept from the people listening, but the text only gives us the request itself. It's a request about language.

Private with Hezekiah isn't what they ask for. Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebnah the scribe and Joah the recorder say, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it.” They ask him not to use Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall. It's all about which language he uses.

No rescheduling in this request. Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebnah the scribe and Joah the recorder say, “Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it.” They want him to switch languages right then. Nobody asks him to check his calendar.

He doesn't agree at all. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, replies, “Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall…” So he says the words are for the men on the wall too. The request gets a firm no.

Right, the request is turned down. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, answers, “Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall…” He says the men on the wall are meant to hear it too. Asking him to keep it quiet didn't work.

That's it. The Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew. Hebrew is the very language the three officials had asked him not to use in the hearing of the people on the wall. Now he's using it at full volume.

explanations.answer: Walks back to the army camp
explanations.explanation: He's not going anywhere, friend. The text says the Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew. He's staying right where the people on the wall can hear him. If he had left, this would be a much shorter chapter.
No letter in this scene. The Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew. He's talking out loud, and the people on the wall are in earshot. Hezekiah isn't getting a note, he's getting a shout.

He says the opposite. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, tells the people, “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; he cannot deliver you from my hand.” That's him telling the crowd on the wall not to count on Hezekiah, their king. It's the first thing he says when he starts shouting.

Yes, he says Hezekiah can't. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, tells the people, “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; he cannot deliver you from my hand.” He's speaking right to the people on the wall. He wants them doubting their own king.

He does warn them. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD when he says, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.’” He's quoting what Hezekiah says and telling the people not to be persuaded by it. That's his line, and he's repeating it to the whole wall.

It's right there in verse 30. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD when he says, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us…’” So he brings up Hezekiah's promise and tells the people not to listen. He's quoting the king back to his own people.

explanations.answer: He will take them to a land like their own
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. After the vine, the fig tree and the cistern, he says, “…until I come and take you away to a land like your own…” So the picture he paints has a move in it. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says it with a smile on his sales pitch.

explanations.answer: He will let them stay in Jerusalem for good
explanations.explanation: Staying isn't in his pitch, friend. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says they can eat from their own vine and fig tree “…until I come and take you away to a land like your own…” That word "until" matters. He's talking about being taken away.

explanations.answer: He will keep Hezekiah in charge of them
explanations.explanation: He's not talking about keeping Hezekiah. In fact the Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, keeps telling them not to listen to Hezekiah. What he says is, “…until I come and take you away to a land like your own…” So the plan is a move, with the king of Assyria in charge.

Samaria is the name he drops. He asks, “Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?” It's a roll call, and Samaria is the last name on it. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, is counting off places like a man reading a very long guest list.

Damascus isn't on his list. He asks, “Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?” The name he lands on is Samaria. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, is rattling off places and gods.

Tyre doesn't make his list, friend. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, asks about Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivvah. Then he asks, “Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?” Samaria is the name that finishes the question.

He does. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, finishes with, “Who among all the gods of these lands has delivered his land from my hand? How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?” He lines up all those place names and then points his question straight at Jerusalem. It's the end of his big speech.

He does ask it, and it's the closing line. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, says, “How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?” Before that he names a whole list of lands. All of it leads up to that one question.

Silence it is. The text says, “But the people remained silent and did not answer a word…” After all that shouting, nobody says a thing. That takes a lot of self-control, friend. I'd have at least cleared my throat.

explanations.answer: They shout right back at him
explanations.explanation: No shouting back. The text says, “But the people remained silent and did not answer a word…” The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian official, does all the talking. The wall stays quiet.
The gates stay shut in this passage. The people on the wall “remained silent and did not answer a word.” They don't give him anything, not even a reply. Nobody opens a thing.

The text gives the reason. The people stayed silent “for Hezekiah had commanded, ‘Do not answer him.’” So their quiet wasn't an accident. Hezekiah, Judah's king, gave an order, and the wall followed it.

The verse gives the reason outright. The people remained silent “for Hezekiah had commanded, ‘Do not answer him.’” Hezekiah, Judah's king, told them ahead of time. So the silence came from his command.

They come to Hezekiah with their clothes torn. That's Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder, the same three who went out to meet the Rabshakeh. The text doesn't say why they tore them. I think the words they heard hit them hard.

Covered heads aren't mentioned. The text says Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder came to Hezekiah “with their clothes torn.” Then they relayed the Rabshakeh's words to him. It's the clothes that tell the story.

The text says nothing about their feet. Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder came to Hezekiah “with their clothes torn.” Their clothes are the detail it gives. After that they tell him what the Rabshakeh said.
